Chapter 1Introduction

1.1 Natural Language Processing

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that helps computers read, understand and use human language. Common uses are chatbots, translation, search engines and question answering.

1.2 Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Document Q&A

Chatbots do not know our private documents and sometimes make up answers. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fixes this in two parts: first the program retrieves the passages of the documents that match the question, then a language model generates a short answer from only those passages. The page number of each passage is shown, so the answer can be checked. Typical uses are study help, company documents and customer support.

1.3 Objective of the Project

The objective is to build Askmargin, a small document question-answering assistant in Python. It should:

  • read four public PDF papers and cut them into small chunks;
  • find the best chunks for a question with two search methods and compare them;
  • write a short answer with an open language model and show the pages used;
  • refuse questions that the documents cannot answer.

Chapter 2Tools and Libraries Used

  • Platform: Google Colab with Python.
  • PyMuPDF: reads the text of PDF files page by page.
  • NLTK: splits text into sentences.
  • scikit-learn: TF-IDF word-matching search.
  • sentence-transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2): turns text into vectors (embeddings) for meaning-based search.
  • Transformers (FLAN-T5-base): small open language model that writes the answer.

Data: four public arXiv papers (Attention Is All You Need, BERT, RAG, Sentence-BERT), 61 pages in total, and 10 test questions with known answers.

Chapter 3Methodology

The system follows seven steps.

  1. Read and clean: read every PDF page with its page number; join hyphenated words and remove extra spaces.
  2. Chunking: split pages into chunks of about 500 characters made of whole sentences.
  3. TF-IDF search: tokenise, remove stop-words and score chunks by matching words.
  4. Embedding search: turn chunks and question into 384 numbers and compare them with cosine similarity.
  5. Compare: test both searches on 10 questions (top-3 accuracy).
  6. Generate: give the best 3 chunks to FLAN-T5 with the instruction to answer only from them; print the sources.
  7. Refuse: if the best similarity is below 0.25, answer "I could not find this in the documents."

Chapter 5Results and Analysis

Table 5.1: Results of the experiments.
Test Result
TF-IDF search, top-3 accuracy (10 questions) 0.9 (9 of 10)
Embedding search, top-3 accuracy (10 questions) 0.9 (9 of 10)
3 questions from the papers 2 correct, 1 wrong
1 question not in the papers refused correctly
  • Both searches found the answer text for 9 of 10 questions, so on this small test neither is clearly better.
  • The answers show the document and page of the chunks used.
  • The question about France was refused instead of answered.
  • The question about the generator model got a wrong answer ("RAG-Token Model", correct is BART); FLAN-T5-base is small and can pick a wrong detail.
  • Only 10 test questions and one refusal example were used, so the results are only indicative.

The same idea is also available as a website, askmargin.vercel.app, which runs in the browser.

Chapter 6Conclusion

Askmargin is a small but complete NLP pipeline: it reads PDFs, cleans and chunks the text, searches with TF-IDF and with embeddings, writes an answer with FLAN-T5 and refuses when the documents do not help. It answered most questions with page references, but it also made a clear mistake, which shows why the page sources matter. In future, a bigger test set and a stronger language model can be used.
